question: Baba ganoush is a Levantine eggplant dip famous for a deep, smoky flavor — and that smokiness isn't from any added spice. Cooks build it by doing one dramatic thing to the whole eggplant before scooping out its soft insides. What do they do to it?
answer: Blacken its skin whole over an open flame
choices: Blacken its skin whole over an open flame
Smoke it for hours in a smokehouse
Brush it with liquid smoke, then bake
Grill it sealed in a foil packet
context: You char the whole eggplant black — held over a gas burner or grill for about 20 minutes — until the skin is completely blistered and the flesh inside collapses to a soft, smoky pulp. Then you scoop it out and mash it with tahini, lemon, garlic and olive oil. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Baba_ghanoush; themediterraneandish.com/baba-ganoush-recipe

question: Labneh is a soft white cheese, spread across plates with olive oil and dried mint all over the Levant — but it's one of the few cheeses made with no rennet and no aging at all. It's really just one everyday dairy food with its liquid strained out. Which dairy food is strained to make labneh?
context: Labneh is strained yogurt: you hang plain yogurt in a cloth bag for hours until the watery whey drips away and it thickens into a spreadable cheese. Rolled into little balls and packed in olive oil (labneh bil zeit), it seals out the air and keeps for over a year without a fridge. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Strained_yogurt

question: Dolma are little parcels of seasoned rice and herbs, and here's the twist — the leaf wrapped around each one isn't peeled off and thrown away. You eat the wrapper right along with the filling. Which leaf does a classic dolma use?
context: Dolma's Arabic name is warak enab — literally 'grape leaves.' The tender vine leaf is simmered soft and eaten with the rice filling, not unwrapped. 'Dolma' comes from Turkish 'dolmak,' to be stuffed or filled; in Turkish, 'sarma' means the rolled-in-leaves kind and 'dolma' the stuffed-vegetable kind. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dolma

question: Muhammara is a brick-red dip from Aleppo, Syria, built on roasted red peppers with a sweet-tart tang. Its rich body and its crunch come from one ground-up nut blended right in. Which nut is it?
context: Muhammara means 'reddened' in Arabic. Ground walnuts give it body and crunch; roasted red peppers and Aleppo pepper bring the color and warmth, pomegranate molasses the sweet-tart tang, and breadcrumbs the thickness. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Muhammara

question: The eggplant behind baba ganoush feels ancient and Mediterranean — but the Greeks and Romans never even had a word for it, because they'd never laid eyes on one. It's really a native of South Asia. Who carried the eggplant west across the Mediterranean, reaching Spain by the 8th century?
context: The eggplant comes from South Asia (India). Medieval Arab traders spread it west across the Mediterranean world, and it reached Spain — then Al-Andalus — in the 8th century. The tell that it was a newcomer: the ancient Greeks and Romans had no name for a plant they had never seen. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eggplant

question: One thick, dark, tangy syrup runs all through Levantine cooking — cooks drizzle it into salad dressings and stir it into dips for a sweet-sour kick. It's made by simmering a single fruit's juice down and down until a whole potful cooks away to a small syrupy pool. Which fruit's juice becomes this syrup?
context: This is pomegranate molasses — pomegranate juice boiled down until it reduces to a dark, tart syrup. It's the sweet-sour backbone of Levantine dressings and the tang hidden inside dips like muhammara. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pomegranate_molasses

question: A steaming bowl of spicy food gets its burn from chili peppers. Surprise: every chili pepper on Earth traces back to wild plants that grew in just one part of the world before sailors carried them everywhere else. Where did chili peppers first come from?
context: Chili peppers grew wild only in the Americas and were unknown across Africa and Asia before Columbus sailed in 1492. From the late 1490s, Portuguese merchants carried Brazilian-grown chilies to West and North Africa, where the heat quickly became a signature of local cooking. Source: Wikipedia, 'Columbian exchange.'

question: Coffee is grown across the world today, but every coffee bush traces back to wild plants that first sprang up on the highlands of one single country. Which country is coffee's original home?
context: Wild Coffea arabica first grew in Ethiopia, and the word 'coffee' traces back to Ethiopia's Kaffa province — so this bean actually traveled OUT of Africa to the rest of the world. A famous legend, not written down before 1671, credits a goatherd who supposedly saw his goats prance with energy after eating the red coffee berries; even the goatherd's usual name, 'Kaldi,' is a 20th-century invention. Source: Wikipedia, 'History of coffee.'

question: Some African foods sailed the other way — to the Americas. The famous Louisiana stew called gumbo takes its very name from ki ngombo, a word carried to the Americas by enslaved Africans, along with the very plant it names. Which vegetable does that word — and the dish — actually name?
context: Okra is native to East Africa (Ethiopia, Eritrea and Sudan) and reached the Americas by 1658, when it was recorded in Brazil. The Louisiana dish name 'gumbo' comes from the Bantu word ki ngombo, meaning okra. Onion, celery and bell pepper — the 'holy trinity' — go into gumbo too, but the word itself means okra. Source: Wikipedia, 'Okra.'

question: Africa's most important staple crop today is maize — the corn ground into ugali, nshima and pap across the continent. But a fat corn cob does not exist in nature; farmers in southern Mexico spent thousands of years breeding it from a scrawny wild grass. What is that wild ancestor grass called?
context: Maize was domesticated about 9,000 years ago from wild teosinte in the Balsas River valley of southern Mexico. Portuguese ships introduced it to Africa in the 16th century, where it became the continent's most important staple — eaten as ugali, nshima, sadza and mieliepap. Source: Wikipedia, 'Maize.'

question: Fufu and garri are everyday staples across West Africa, both made from the starchy cassava root — a plant that came from Brazil. There is a catch: raw cassava is naturally poisonous. Before it is safe to eat, West African cooks must first do what to the root?
answer: Soak the roots in water to ferment
choices: Soak the roots in water to ferment
Boil the roots once in salted water
Peel the tough skin off the roots
context: Cassava (manioc) is native to west-central Brazil and was brought to Africa by Portuguese traders in the 16th century, where it became a top staple. Raw cassava root is naturally toxic; West Africans make it safe by soaking the roots in water for about three days to ferment before drying or cooking, or by grating and lightly frying it in palm oil into garri. Source: Wikipedia, 'Cassava.'

question: Jollof rice is the pride of West African cooking — a one-pot rice dish stained deep red with tomatoes and tomato paste, and cooks in Ghana and Nigeria argue endlessly over whose pot is best. Portuguese ships landed the tomato in Africa about 500 years ago. Roughly how old is the tomato-based jollof that West Africans cook today?
context: A crop's arrival and a dish's birth are two different dates. The tomato is the red heart of jollof rice, but tomatoes, tomato paste and capsicum (chili) peppers are all New World crops that reached Africa only after Columbus — and the modern tomato-based jollof dates only to about the 19th century, roughly three centuries after the tomato itself landed. Jollof takes its name from the Wolof people of Senegal. Source: Wikipedia, 'Jollof rice.'

question: Italy's kitchens split by fat. In the cool north near the Alps, cooks fry and finish their dishes with a fat the sunny south uses far less. Which fat leads the northern kitchen?
context: Broadly, the north of Italy — Emilia-Romagna and the Alpine belt — cooks with butter (and cream) from its cattle pastures, while central and southern Italy reach for olive oil. It's a tendency, not a hard border. Source: Wikipedia, 'Italian cuisine' (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Italian_cuisine).

question: Up north in Bologna, fresh tagliatelle glows a silky golden-yellow; down south, dried spaghetti is pale and firm. One ingredient in the northern dough — left out of the southern version entirely — makes that difference. What is it?
context: Northern Italy specializes in fresh egg pasta — pasta all'uovo — like tagliatelle and filled tortellini, classic to Emilia-Romagna and Bologna. Southern dried pasta (pasta secca) is just durum-wheat semolina and water, no egg. Source: Wikipedia, 'Italian cuisine' (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Italian_cuisine).

question: Dried pasta keeps for months on the shelf, and in Italy it became the SOUTH's everyday staple, not the north's. What let southern Sicily and Puglia turn out dried pasta while the north could not?
answer: Hot, dry winds that air-dried the pasta while the humid north stayed too damp
choices: Hot, dry winds that air-dried the pasta while the humid north stayed too damp
Wealthy nobles who paid to stockpile food that poorer northerners could not
A shortage of fresh eggs that forced southern cooks to dry their dough
Ancient Roman laws that reserved fresh pasta for the northern cities
context: Durum ('hard') wheat thrives in the hot, dry south, and Sicily's hot, dry winds were ideal for air-drying pasta so it keeps; the cooler, wetter, humid north grew soft wheat and was too damp to air-dry pasta, so it ate fresh pasta the same day. Source: The Thinking Traveller, 'Pasta traditions in Sicily and Puglia'.

question: In the northern mountains, poor families of Piemonte and Veneto lived for generations on polenta — a thick porridge slow-cooked for hours from the ground meal of a single crop. Which crop fed them?
context: Polenta — slow-cooked ground corn (maize) — has been a peasant staple of northern Italy for centuries, standard across Piemonte, Lombardia, Veneto and Friuli. The north's other non-pasta starch is risotto: creamy short-grain rice grown on the Po Valley plains, watered by Alpine snowmelt. Source: La Cucina Italiana, 'Polenta'.

question: Olive oil already ruled the southern Italian kitchen, but one turn of medieval history deepened its hold for good. What gave olive oil an extra boost across the south in the Middle Ages?
answer: Lenten fasting rules banned animal fats like butter, and oil broke no rule
choices: Lenten fasting rules banned animal fats like butter, and oil broke no rule
Arab traders brought the first olive presses across the sea to Sicily
A cattle plague wiped out the south's dairy herds for a generation
Roman emperors taxed butter heavily as a foreign northern luxury
context: During Lent the Catholic Church banned animal fats such as butter and lard, and the south already had olive oil on hand — a fat that fit the rule — which reinforced oil's grip on southern cooking (a contributing factor, told as culinary history). Source: Mortadella Head, 'Butter vs olive oil'.

question: The north-south split runs through the cheese board too. The northern plains sit on rich dairy pastures with milk to spare — so how do their cheesemakers turn all that milk into Parmigiano and Grana Padano?
answer: By aging the wheels for years until hard and grateable
choices: By aging the wheels for years until hard and grateable
By stretching the warm curd into soft ropes by hand
By curdling it and eating it fresh within a day
By smoking the young cheese over smouldering wood
context: The north ages hard cow's-milk cheeses — Parmigiano Reggiano and Grana Padano, whose name 'Padano' points to the Po Valley (Pianura Padana). The south instead makes fresh stretched-curd (pasta filata) cheeses — mozzarella, burrata, provolone; true Mozzarella di Bufala Campana is at its best within 24 hours of being made. Sources: Wikipedia, 'Parmesan'; Nonna Box, 'Italian cheeses'.

question: Cut an onion in half and it splits into neat concentric rings, one nested inside the next. Each of those rings is really one of the onion's fattened ___?
context: An onion is a bulb: a short, squat, compressed underground stem wrapped in concentric fleshy 'scale' leaves. Every ring you slice through is one of those swollen storage leaves seen end-on — the onion is a stack of fat leaf-bases, not a solid root. (Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Onion)

question: An onion's papery brown skin peels away in crackly sheets, looking nothing like the moist flesh underneath. What is that brown skin, really?
answer: a set of outer layers, dried brittle with age
choices: a set of outer layers, dried brittle with age
a waxy rind that seals in the bulb's water
a papery husk left behind by the flower
a crust of soil baked hard onto the bulb
context: The dry, papery skin on an onion is just its outermost leaves — the same storage leaves as the juicy rings, but the outer ones dried out and went brittle as the bulb matured, forming a protective wrapper. (Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Onion)

question: Chop into a raw onion and within seconds your eyes water and sting. The slicing tears open the onion's cells and lets loose something that drifts up to your eyes and irritates them. What is it?
answer: a tiny cloud of sulfur gas
choices: a tiny cloud of sulfur gas
a fine mist of onion acid
context: Cutting an onion ruptures its cells, releasing an enzyme (alliinase) that turns the onion's stored sulfur compounds into a tiny, volatile sulfur gas — the chemical syn-propanethial-S-oxide. It drifts up to your eyes, irritates them, and your eyes make tears to wash it away. The food-level answer is 'a sulfur gas'; the tongue-twister chemical name is only trivia. (Sources: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Onion; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Syn-Propanethial-S-oxide)

question: A head of garlic breaks apart into a cluster of cloves, each wrapped in its own papery jacket. A gardener wanting more garlic simply pushes one single clove down into the soil. What grows up from that one clove?
context: A garlic bulb (a 'head') splits into 10-20 cloves, and each clove is itself a tiny complete storage bud wrapped in a papery leaf — plant just one clove and it grows an entire new plant. Garlic mostly copies itself this way instead of making seeds. (Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Garlic)

question: A whole, unbroken garlic clove held to your nose barely smells of anything. Yet the instant you crush or chop it, a fierce garlicky punch appears. Where does that sudden smell come from?
answer: from a chemical reaction that builds it on the spot
choices: from a chemical reaction that builds it on the spot
from oily droplets that burst under the knife
from the papery skin as it splits open
from juice squeezed out of the broken cells
context: Whole, unbroken garlic barely smells. The sharp garlic punch only appears the instant you crush or chop it: that breaks the cells and lets the enzyme alliinase convert odorless 'alliin' into pungent 'allicin' — the smell is literally manufactured on the spot by the damage. (Sources: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Garlic; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Allicin)

question: Raw garlic is fierce: bite a raw clove and it burns and stings the tongue. But leave a whole head of garlic to roast slowly in the oven, and something happens to that fierce bite. What becomes of it once the garlic is roasted soft?
answer: it mellows into something mild and sweet
choices: it mellows into something mild and sweet
it sharpens into something even fiercer
it sours into something harsh and metallic
it fades but stays just as sharp
context: Heat tames the alliums. Cooking breaks down the sharp compound (allicin), so raw garlic bites hard but roasted garlic turns mild, sweet, brown and jammy. The enzyme that makes the pungent compound is also destroyed by heat, so cooked garlic can't keep generating its own sharpness. (Sources: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Garlic; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Allicin)

question: It feels personal when an onion makes you sob over the cutting board, but the onion never aimed its eye-watering chemistry at you. Biologists say a wild onion or garlic bulb, sitting buried underground, evolved that harsh, pungent chemistry to do one real job. What job?
answer: to poison and repel pests that gnaw at the bulb
choices: to poison and repel pests that gnaw at the bulb
to help the bulb store water through a drought
to lure in insects that spread its pollen
to stop the buried bulb freezing in winter
context: The tears aren't an accident — they're the plant fighting back. Onions and garlic evolved their pungent sulfur chemistry as a defense: those compounds repel and even poison insects, herbivores, slugs, snails, nematodes, and fungi that would eat the bulb. Your crying is a byproduct of a chemical weapon meant for pests. (Sources: Frontiers in Plant Science, 2024; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Allicin)

question: Long before any ship sailed around Africa to reach them, pepper, cinnamon and cloves already arrived in Europe — carried thousands of miles overland across Asia in long, plodding trains loaded with sacks of spice. Which animals made up those spice caravans?
context: Long before sea routes, spices moved by land: great camel caravans crossed Asia's deserts loaded with pepper, cinnamon and cloves, hauling them thousands of miles toward the Mediterranean. Source: blog.der-leiermann.com, corroborated by Wikipedia 'Spice trade' and Grokipedia 'Spice trade'.

question: For some 700 years, almost every peppercorn, cinnamon stick and clove that reached Europe crossed the docks of a single Italian city, which grew fabulously rich as the whole continent's spice gateway. Which city was it?
context: From roughly the 8th to the 15th century the Italian maritime republics — above all Venice — held a near-monopoly on European trade with the East, so almost every Eastern spice entered Europe through Venetian docks. Source: Wikipedia 'Spice trade', corroborated by Smithsonian Magazine.

question: In the medieval spice trade, a merchant weighing out true cinnamon could set it on his scales against an equal weight of a certain metal and call the swap a fair, even trade. Pound for pound, cinnamon was reckoned worth about as much as which metal?
context: Cinnamon was so precious that a single kilogram of it cost about as much as a kilogram of silver — gold was dearer still, which is why it makes the tempting wrong guess. Source: blog.der-leiermann.com.

question: A sack of black pepper bought for a handful of coins on India's coast was worth about THIRTY times as much by the time it reached Europe's markets — a fortune that grew at every stop as the cargo passed from one set of merchant hands to the next. Which two groups of middlemen guarded most of that spice fortune?
context: Pepper bought for a handful of coins on India's Malabar Coast sold for about TEN times as much once Arab merchants had carried it west to the Mediterranean, and roughly THIRTY times its starting price by the time Venetian merchants shipped it on to Venice — so it was that relay of Arab and then Venetian middlemen, not the Ottomans who later seized the crossroads, the Portuguese who wanted in, or Venice's Genoese rivals, who guarded the spice fortune. Escaping exactly that markup is what later sent European captains hunting for a sea route of their own. Source: blog.der-leiermann.com, markup stages corroborated by mexicohistorico.com.

question: In 1453 the Ottoman Turks captured Constantinople, the crossroads city on the overland spice road, and cooks across Europe braced for pepper to price itself out of their kitchens. It never happened — for the next forty-five years Europe's pepper prices barely moved, because Venice had quietly kept its own supply open. Who was Venice buying its pepper from?
context: The 1453 fall of Constantinople was a SQUEEZE, not a total blockade: historian A.H. Lybyer showed in 1915 that European pepper prices did not jump sharply between 1453 and 1498, because Venice kept buying through a treaty with the Mamluks of Alexandria (who charged about a 33% export tariff). The real crack came in 1498, when Vasco da Gama reached Calicut on India's Malabar Coast by sea and carried pepper home the direct way — that flood of cheaper spice roughly halved Venice's pepper prices and broke the centuries-old monopoly. Source: blog.der-leiermann.com; Wikipedia 'Fall of Constantinople'; Lybyer 1915 via gertitashkomd.com.

question: Passion flowers and passion fruit sound like they're named for romance, but the Spanish and Portuguese missionaries who met the vine in South America in the 1500s meant something far darker. To them, 'the Passion' named one particular ordeal from their faith. Which was it?
context: The word 'passion' comes from the Latin passio, meaning suffering, so 'the Passion' is the suffering and death of Jesus on the cross. Spanish and Portuguese missionaries in the Americas in the 1500s and 1600s saw the story of Christ's death in the strange flower and named it for that; it has nothing to do with romantic love. (Sources: University of Dayton Marian Library, 'Passion Flower'; Wikipedia, 'Passiflora'.)

question: The passion flower isn't the only gift of its vine — the same plant produces the passion fruit, a South American favorite. In Brazil the tart, musky pulp is whipped into a fluffy mousse and spooned over cakes. What do Brazilians call this fruit?
context: In Brazil the fruit is maracujá, from the Tupi word murukuia. Its tart pulp — wrapped around roughly 250 seeds — flavors juice, mousse, and desserts, and passion-fruit mousse is a classic Brazilian sweet. The vine, Passiflora edulis, is native to southern Brazil, Paraguay, and northern Argentina. (Source: Wikipedia, 'Passiflora edulis'.)

question: The missionaries who met the passion flower in South America read Christ's suffering into it part by part. The feature at the very heart of the bloom — the one that first grabs your eye — took one specific role from the Crucifixion story. What did they say it stood for?
context: The frilly fringe is called the corona, and in some species it is a ring of 70 to 100 or more colored threads. To the missionaries it stood for the crown of thorns pressed onto Christ's head, and it is the flower's most striking feature. (Sources: University of Dayton Marian Library, 'Passion Flower'; Wikipedia, 'Passiflora'.)  (Legend.)

question: Cashews, almonds, and pecans all get lumped together and called nuts, and the peanut borrows the word too — but it isn't a nut at all, it's a cousin of some very familiar garden plants. Which family does the peanut really belong to?
context: Botanists file the peanut in Fabaceae, the legume family — the same clan as beans, peas, and lentils. Its seeds grow inside a pod, exactly like peas in a pea pod, which is why it breaks every rule for a true 'nut.' Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peanut

question: Peanuts feel deeply Southern — boiled at county fairs, roasted at ballgames. Yet the plant isn't native to North America at all; Spanish and Portuguese ships first carried it out of its true homeland, half a world away. Where did the peanut originally grow wild?
answer: east of the Andes, in South America
choices: east of the Andes, in South America
in the river valleys of India
across the islands of Southeast Asia
context: The peanut grew wild east of the Andes — around Peru, Bolivia, Argentina, and Brazil. Spanish and Portuguese traders carried it to Africa, and it returned to North America on slave ships. That African detour marked our language: the Southern word 'goober' comes from 'nguba,' the Kongo word for the plant. Sources: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peanut; npr.org/sections/codeswitch (2014-04-20)

question: A peanut plant blooms with small yellow flowers up in the open air — but you will never find a peanut hanging on the plant above the ground. After one of those flowers is pollinated, what does the plant do to turn that flower into a peanut?
answer: A stalk grows from the flower and pushes the young pod down into the soil.
choices: A stalk grows from the flower and pushes the young pod down into the soil.
The flower's petals harden into a shell around the seeds on the stem.
The whole plant leans over until its flowers touch the ground.
The wind scatters the seeds, and new pods sprout where they land.
context: That downward-growing stalk is called the 'peg' (a gynophore, growing from the base of the flower's ovary). It drives the fertilized pod straight into the ground, where the peanuts ripen in the dark — shielded from animals and weather. Botanists call this rare trick geocarpy, 'fruit in the earth.' Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peanut

question: The peanut's yellow flower opens for only a single day before it withers. In that one short day, how does the flower manage to get pollinated at all?
answer: It pollinates itself, needing no other flower.
choices: It pollinates itself, needing no other flower.
It draws in a single kind of bee that visits only peanuts.
It relies on ants to carry pollen up its stem.
It casts its pollen on the wind to reach other blooms.
context: The peanut's yellow flower is self-pollinating and lasts only about a day. Once pollinated, it withers and its peg begins the long push down into the soil to ripen the pod underground. Source: biologyinsights.com/are-peanuts-roots-the-science-behind-underground-pods

question: Plant cotton in the same field year after year and the soil goes dead — the crop keeps stripping something vital from the dirt. Plant peanuts there one season, and next spring's corn comes up thick and tall with no fertilizer at all. What are the peanut's roots quietly doing down in the soil?
answer: Pulling nitrogen out of the air and locking it into the soil.
choices: Pulling nitrogen out of the air and locking it into the soil.
Rotting fallen leaves into a rich compost around their roots.
Drawing deep buried minerals up toward the topsoil.
Feeding the soil's earthworms with sugars from their roots.
context: Because it's a legume, the peanut houses symbiotic bacteria (rhizobia) in nodules on its roots. They pull nitrogen straight from the air and fix it into the ground, refilling land that crops like cotton and corn drain — which is why peanuts are prized in crop rotation. The payoff is measurable: in Texas, peanuts grown in a three-year rotation with corn yield about 50% more than peanuts grown on the same land every year. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peanut

question: George Washington Carver — born into slavery, later a scientist at Tuskegee — urged Southern farmers to plant soil-rebuilding peanuts where cotton had worn the land out. It worked too well: farmers were soon buried in peanuts nobody would buy. Carver's answer, the work that made his name, was to do what?
answer: Invent hundreds of new peanut products, from flour to glue to shaving cream.
choices: Invent hundreds of new peanut products, from flour to glue to shaving cream.
Build the South's first factory for turning peanuts into peanut butter.
Ship the leftover peanuts across the ocean to sell them in Europe.
Breed a bigger, sweeter peanut that shoppers would pay more for.
context: The Carver Museum at Tuskegee credited George Washington Carver with roughly 300 peanut uses (it counted 287) — milk, flour, dyes, paints, cosmetics, glue, even shaving cream. In 1921 he testified before Congress's House Ways and Means Committee, unpacking product after product; congressmen who came to mock him kept extending his time to hear more. One thing he did NOT do was invent peanut butter — a Canadian pharmacist, Marcellus Gilmore Edson, patented a peanut paste in 1884 (twelve years before Carver reached Tuskegee), and peanut pastes go back to the Aztecs. Carver was the peanut's great promoter and popularizer, not the inventor of its most famous product. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Washington_Carver

question: The very first pies weren't sweet at all — a hunk of meat sealed inside a thick, rock-hard shell of flour and water that held the filling together in the oven. What did medieval English bakers call that stiff crust?
context: The word was 'coffyn,' and it simply meant a basket or box — nothing to do with burial. It named the crust's shape, not a graveyard. These early coffins were savory: a shell of rye flour and water baked several inches thick around the meat, made to survive hours in the oven. Source: Wikipedia, 'Pie'; Matador Network, 'Coffin-Inspired History of Pie Crust.'

question: Long before refrigerators existed, a baked meat pie could ride in a saddlebag for weeks and still be good to eat — and the crust was the reason. How did that thick, rock-hard shell keep the meat inside from spoiling?
answer: it locked the air away from the meat
choices: it locked the air away from the meat
it drew the moisture out of the meat
it packed salt tight against the meat
it baked the meat sterile in the oven
context: With no air reaching it, the trapped meat and its juices couldn't spoil, so a sealed pie kept for weeks — historians have nicknamed the coffin crust 'medieval Tupperware.' Bakers sometimes poured melted fat through a hole in the top crust to plug out the last of the air. Source: Atlas Obscura, 'Who Made the First Pie?'; Matador Network, 'Coffin-Inspired History of Pie Crust.'

question: A traditional English pork pie stands up all on its own — no tin, no dish — its thick pastry walls holding a heavy, juicy filling without slumping. The secret is how the dough is mixed: unlike ordinary pastry, this one is made with ___?
choices: beaten eggs stirred into soft flour
yeast dough left to rise overnight
olive oil worked into fine semolina
context: This is 'hot-water crust.' Melting fat into boiling water and beating in the flour makes a hot, pliable paste a baker can 'hand-raise' into free-standing walls; as it bakes and cools it sets firm enough to hold a wet, heavy filling. A Melton Mowbray pork pie is shaped by hand around a wooden mould and baked with no tin at all, which is why it bulges into its famous bowed shape. Source: Wikipedia, 'Hot water crust pastry'; National Geographic, 'Melton Mowbray pork pies.'

question: Every pie-crust recipe barks the same rule: keep the butter cold, work fast, don't let it soften in your warm hands. What does that cold fat do once the crust hits the hot oven?
answer: the fat melts and its water flashes to steam, prying layers apart
choices: the fat melts and its water flashes to steam, prying layers apart
the fat melts and fries the dough crisp from the inside out
the fat melts and coats the flour, keeping the crumb tender
the fat melts and soaks in, baking the dough rich and dense
context: Kept cold, the fat stays in solid flakes between sheets of dough instead of blending in. In the oven those flakes melt, and the water trapped inside the butter — along with the moisture in the dough — flashes to steam and pries the layers apart into hundreds of thin, crisp pockets. The fat itself never turns to steam; it just melts, leaving the gaps the steam puffs open. One warning: shortcrust uses about twice as much flour as fat, and if you overwork the dough you build up gluten and it turns tough and chewy instead of tender. Source: Wikipedia, 'Shortcrust pastry.'

question: You're pre-baking an empty pie crust so a wet filling won't leave it soggy, but an empty crust puffs up and slumps in the heat. The old cook's fix is to line it with paper and fill it with something heavy that you tip back out afterward. What do bakers traditionally weigh an empty crust down with?
context: This is called 'blind baking' — pre-baking a crust empty. Bakers line it with parchment and pour in dried beans, rice, or ceramic 'pie weights' to stop the pastry from bubbling up or slumping, then lift them out before adding the filling. A quicker fix is 'docking': pricking the raw crust all over with a fork so trapped steam escapes through the holes instead of doming the base. Source: Wikipedia, 'Blind-baking.'

question: 'As American as apple pie' — except the apple isn't American at all. It's an Old World fruit that European settlers carried across the Atlantic; only sour little crab apples grew wild in North America before they came. So which classic pie is filled with a crop that really is native to the Americas, grown by Indigenous farmers for thousands of years before any settler arrived?
context: Apple pie is actually medieval English, not American: the oldest known recipe, 'For to make Tartys in Applis,' appears in 'The Forme of Cury' (about 1381), written by King Richard II's cooks — and it tells you to bake the apples in a 'cofyn,' the very same coffin crust. The apple's wild ancestor still grows in the mountains of Kazakhstan and rode the Silk Road toward Europe long before reaching America. Pumpkin, though, is a true New World squash domesticated in Mexico thousands of years ago — one of the 'Three Sisters' grown with corn and beans. Source: Wikipedia, 'Apple' & 'Pumpkin'; Tasting History, 'Medieval Apple Pie'; The Forme of Cury (c.1381).

question: Almonds, walnuts, and peanuts all get sold in the shell for you to crack open yourself — but a cashew never does. What's the problem with a raw, untreated cashew shell?
answer: It's coated in a caustic oil that blisters skin.
choices: It's coated in a caustic oil that blisters skin.
It's so hard that no home nutcracker can open it.
It gives off a smell that spoils the nut inside.
It hides a bitter second seed that tastes soapy.
context: The raw cashew shell is coated in a caustic oil, chemically related to poison ivy's, that blisters and burns bare skin. That's why cashews are always shelled and heat-treated at the factory before you ever see them — you never buy a cashew in its shell. Source: Wikipedia, 'Cashew'; Scientific American, 'What Do Cashews, Mangoes and Poison Ivy Have in Common?'

question: Some people who bite straight into a mango without peeling it get an itchy rash around their mouth — a mild version of the rash you'd get from brushing a certain plant on a woodland hike. The mango is a close cousin of which plant?
context: A mango's skin, sap and leaves carry urushiol — the very same rash-causing oil as poison ivy — because the two plants are close cousins in the cashew family. So an itchy mouth from unpeeled mango is a real, mild poison-ivy reaction; peeling the fruit removes the irritant. Source: Wikipedia, 'Mango'; Scientific American, 'What Do Cashews, Mangoes and Poison Ivy Have in Common?'

question: Those bags labeled 'raw cashews' at the health-food store aren't quite what they claim: every commercial cashew has already been treated to destroy the caustic oil in its shell. What is done to each and every one?
answer: It's roasted at high heat to burn off the shell oil.
choices: It's roasted at high heat to burn off the shell oil.
It's soaked in vinegar to dissolve the shell oil.
It's bathed in limewater to neutralize the shell oil.
It's boiled in plain water to rinse the shell oil away.
context: 'Raw' cashews are a bit of a myth — every commercial cashew is steamed or drum-roasted to destroy the caustic oil in its shell, a step that also makes the tough shell brittle enough to crack open. Source: Wikipedia, 'Cashew'; cashew-processing industry guides.

question: Sumac — the tangy, sour, lemony spice sprinkled over Middle Eastern dishes and stirred into za'atar — grows on a shrub in the same family as cashews and poison ivy. There's also a poison sumac cousin you must never eat. Out in the wild, how do you tell the edible shrub from the poisonous one?
answer: The edible one has red berries; poison sumac has white.
choices: The edible one has red berries; poison sumac has white.
The edible one has thorns; poison sumac has none.
The edible one smells of lemon; poison sumac is odorless.
The edible one has broad leaves; poison sumac has needles.
context: Culinary sumac (Rhus coriaria) grows clusters of red berries and is a safe, tangy spice; poison sumac is a different, toxic cousin, told apart by its white berries. Both belong to the same family as cashews and mangoes. Source: Wikipedia, 'Sumac'.

question: Factories don't throw away the caustic oil in cashew shells — they press it out by the ton and sell it as an industrial raw material. One of these everyday products is really built partly from cashew-shell oil. Which one?
context: Cashew nutshell liquid (CNSL) is a real industrial raw material — its tough resin goes into brake linings and friction materials, plus varnishes, resins and paints. The same seed gives us a snack food and a car part. Source: Wikipedia, 'Cashew' and 'Cashew nutshell liquid'.

question: Pull up a potato plant and the potatoes hang underground, fat with the starch the plant stored in them. Each potato is really a swollen, thickened piece of one plant organ. Which organ is a potato?
context: Botanists call a potato a 'stem tuber.' Tubers form at the swelling tips of long, thin underground stems called stolons, which the plant stuffs with starch to store energy - so a potato is a swollen stem, not a root. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Potato

question: Every potato is dotted with little dimples set in a spiral, and gardeners call them the potato's 'eyes.' Leave a potato too long and pale shoots push out of these dimples. What is each 'eye,' in plant terms?
context: Each 'eye' is a bud, exactly like the buds spaced along an above-ground stem - more evidence that a potato is really a stem. A bud is a dormant growth point that can wake up and push out a new shoot. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Potato

question: The potato tastes like the soul of European cooking - Irish champ, German dumplings, British chips - yet the plant only reached Europe about 500 years ago. People first dug up and tamed wild potatoes thousands of years earlier, high in one cold mountain range. Which mountains gave the world the potato?
context: Farmers first domesticated the potato in the Andes of southern Peru and northwestern Bolivia, near Lake Titicaca, roughly 7,000-10,000 years ago - thousands of years before it reached Europe after Columbus. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Potato

question: A carrot starts from a scatter of tiny seeds. A potato is grown a stranger way: plant the right part in spring, and a whole new plant rises from it. To raise next year's crop, what does a farmer actually put in the ground?
context: Growers plant 'seed potatoes' - whole tubers or cut pieces, each carrying at least one eye (bud) - not true seeds. The new plants are clones of the parent. That is why people say you grow potatoes from potatoes. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Potato

question: At a market in the Peruvian highlands you can buy more than four thousand kinds of native potato - far more than the handful of types in a Western supermarket. Their most startling feature is colour: many are shades you would never expect a potato to be. What colours do these native potatoes come in?
context: More than 4,000 varieties of native potato still grow in the Andean highlands (about 3,000 in Peru alone), in reds, purples, blues and golds. The International Potato Center in Lima keeps the world's largest collection, with over 7,000 samples. Source: cipotato.org/potato/native-potato-varieties/

question: High on the freezing Andean plateau, centuries before refrigerators, farmers turned fresh potatoes into 'chuño' - a dried food that keeps for decades and once fed Inca armies on the march. Each night the potatoes froze solid; by day, under the strong sun, the farmers forced the water out of them. How did they squeeze the water out?
answer: they trod on them with their feet
choices: they trod on them with their feet
they pressed them under heavy stones
they wrung them out in cloth
they scraped them with sharp knives
context: This freeze-dried potato is called 'chuño.' On the high plateau (above 3,800 m) the potatoes freeze in the roughly -5C night, then people tread the water out under the day's sun. Chuño keeps for decades and fed Inca soldiers on the march. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chuño

question: It seems obvious that a sweet potato is just a sweeter kind of potato. It is not: the two are only distant cousins from different plant families. The ordinary potato belongs to the nightshade family, but the sweet potato is a close relative of a familiar flowering garden plant. Which flower is the sweet potato related to?
context: A sweet potato is the swollen storage ROOT of Ipomoea batatas, in the morning-glory family (Convolvulaceae). A true potato is a stem tuber in the nightshade family - so despite the shared name, the two are different organs of barely-related plants. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sweet_potato

question: Hardly anyone has ever seen a potato's fruit, because the plants are usually dug up before they finish flowering. But a potato plant does bloom, and above ground it sets small, round, green fruits full of seeds - fruits that look uncannily like a miniature version of another garden favourite. What does a potato's fruit resemble?
context: A potato plant does flower and set fruit: small green berries that look like tiny green tomatoes - no coincidence, since potato and tomato are both nightshades. Each berry holds about 300 true seeds, but the fruits are toxic and are never eaten. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Potato

question: Everyone knows to be wary of a green potato, and most people assume that green colour is itself the poison. Food scientists say that common idea is wrong. So what is the green tinge on a potato, really?
context: The green is chlorophyll - harmless in itself - made as the potato sits in light. But that same light exposure signals the tuber has built up solanine, a natural toxin the nightshade family makes. Because 30-80% of the solanine sits in and just under the skin, cutting the green away or peeling removes most of it. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Solanine

question: When the potato first reached Europe, many people flatly refused to eat it. It grew hidden in the dark soil, it belonged to the poisonous nightshade family, and it was named nowhere in the Bible - so folk decided it must be unclean and dangerous. What fearful nickname did wary Europeans pin on the potato?
context: Because the potato was an unfamiliar nightshade that grew hidden underground and went unmentioned in the Bible, wary Europeans nicknamed it the 'devil's apples' and shunned it as unclean before it slowly became a staple. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_the_potato  (Legend.)

question: One European ruler was so certain the potato could end famine that in 1756 he ordered his distrustful peasants to plant it right across his kingdom - and grateful admirers are said to leave potatoes on his grave to this very day. Which ruler championed the potato this way?
context: Frederick the Great of Prussia issued his 'potato order' in 1756 to guard against famine, earning the nickname 'Kartoffelkönig' - the potato king. Admirers still leave potatoes on his grave, a custom that lives on today. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_the_potato  (Legend.)

question: After Columbus, ships carried the Andean potato across the Atlantic, and within two centuries it had become a staple that helped Europe's population surge. Farmers embraced it over the wheat and barley they had always grown for one blunt, practical reason. What advantage did a field of potatoes have over a field of grain?
answer: it grew far more food per acre
choices: it grew far more food per acre
context: An acre of potatoes yields enormous calories - about 95 gigajoules per hectare, beating maize (78) and rice (77). Economists credit the potato with a large share of the population growth and city-building across Europe and Asia between 1700 and 1900. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Potato

question: When a potato disease swept Ireland in 1845, it did not merely dent the harvest - it destroyed nearly the whole crop, and about a million people starved. The disaster was so complete for one reason: Ireland's poor had come to live on a single kind of potato, the 'Lumper,' grown everywhere as identical clones. Why did depending on one cloned variety turn a crop disease into a catastrophe?
answer: every plant was equally defenceless, so all rotted together
choices: every plant was equally defenceless, so all rotted together
the clones grew too slowly to harvest in time
the single variety drained the soil of its nutrients
the identical plants drew swarms of hungry insects
context: The blight was Phytophthora infestans, a water mould (not a true fungus), which struck from 1845 to 1852; 1847 is remembered as 'Black '47.' With no genetic variety among the cloned Lumpers, the whole crop failed at once. About 1 million people died and 1-2 million emigrated. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Famine_(Ireland)

question: People often call the potato an Irish food, but it isn't Irish at all. It was first farmed thousands of years ago by people living high in one great mountain range, far across the world. Which range was the potato's true home?
context: The potato was first domesticated high in the Andes, around Lake Titicaca on the border of today's Peru and Bolivia, roughly 7,000-10,000 years ago, from wild tubers of the Solanum brevicaule complex. The oldest hard evidence of potato-eating comes from Jiskairumoko in Peru's Titicaca basin, about 12,000 feet up, dated to roughly 3,400-2,200 BC. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Potato.

question: A supermarket sells maybe five kinds of potato. But in the potato's original mountain homeland, farmers still grow more than 4,000 different native varieties, and one thing about them stuns first-time visitors. What astonishes them most?
answer: They come in bright reds, purples, and blues
choices: They come in bright reds, purples, and blues
They grow as large as ripe watermelons
They ripen into sweet red berries like fruit
They climb overhead on tall leafy vines
context: More than 4,000 varieties of native potato still grow in the Andean highlands of Peru, Bolivia, and Ecuador - a rainbow of shapes and colors bred over centuries to survive at 3,500-4,200 meters (about 11,000-14,000 feet). Source: cipotato.org/potato/native-potato-varieties/.

question: After 1750 Europe's poor turned field after field over from grain to potatoes, and the switch spread astonishingly fast. What did the potato do that wheat and rye could not?
answer: Feed far more people from the same ground
choices: Feed far more people from the same ground
Ripen a second full crop every autumn
Keep for years in a dry sack indoors
Grow well in salty soil beside the sea
context: An acre of potatoes yields far more food energy than an acre of grain - about 95 gigajoules per hectare versus wheat's 31 (it beats maize's 78 and rice's 77 too). Those cheap, dense calories are the main reason Europe's poor took it up, and it became a major field crop after 1750. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Potato.

question: The potato belongs to the nightshade family - the same plant family as deadly nightshade, one of history's most infamous poisons. Two beloved dinner vegetables are close cousins of the potato in that same family. Which pair?
context: The potato is a nightshade (family Solanaceae) - the same plant family as deadly nightshade, the tomato, and the eggplant. The tuber is a safe, everyday food; the family reputation comes from wild relatives. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Potato.

question: To turn fresh potatoes into a food that keeps for years, Andean families spread them across the high, flat ground and spend more than a week pressing all the water out of the piles. How do they crush the potatoes to squeeze the water out?
answer: They stomp them with bare feet
choices: They stomp them with bare feet
They roll heavy stones across them
They pound them with wooden clubs
They wring them in leather sacks
context: To make chuno, families gather on flat ground and stomp the potatoes with their bare feet - almost dancing on the piles - to crush out the water and rub off the skins, repeated over more than a week. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chuno.

question: France was the potato's stubbornest foe, sneering that it was food fit only for pigs. In 1748 the French government went further and outright banned the crop, convinced it caused a dreaded disease. Which disease were potatoes wrongly blamed for spreading?
context: France dismissed the potato as pig food and, in 1748, actually banned it - blaming it for causing leprosy. The ban stood until 1772, when the Paris Faculty of Medicine finally declared potatoes fit to eat. Source: nationalgeographic.com/history/article/potato-history-france-western-europe.

question: The potato's cheap calories didn't just fill hungry stomachs. Economists Nathan Nunn and Nancy Qian added up the numbers and found the humble spud drove roughly a quarter of ALL the Old World's growth between 1700 and 1900 - and that growth showed up in two things at once. Which pair did the potato help swell?
context: Economists Nathan Nunn and Nancy Qian calculated that the potato was responsible for about a quarter of the growth in Old World population and urbanization between 1700 and 1900 - one imported vegetable helped build modern Europe's cities. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Potato (citing Nunn & Qian, Quarterly Journal of Economics 126(2), 2011, pp. 593-650).

question: Even after the ban lifted, the French still would not eat potatoes. On a field granted by King Louis XVI, the army pharmacist Antoine-Augustin Parmentier planted a crop of them and set out to make his countrymen want it. How did Parmentier get villagers planting potatoes in their own gardens?
answer: He posted armed guards by day, then let thieves take the crop at night
choices: He posted armed guards by day, then let thieves take the crop at night
He sold seed potatoes so cheaply that poor farmers would plant them
He handed out free tubers so that every village would grow its own
He served potato dishes at court so the fashion would reach the poor
context: As the famous story goes, to make the potato fashionable Antoine-Augustin Parmentier planted a field on land granted by Louis XVI and posted armed guards over it by day - then pulled them off at night so curious locals would sneak in and steal the 'valuable' crop for their own gardens. Parmentier had first eaten potatoes as a French army pharmacist held prisoner by the Prussians during the Seven Years' War - the food the French fed only to hogs kept him alive, and he became its champion. He later threw banquets of about twenty potato dishes for guests including Benjamin Franklin and the chemist Antoine Lavoisier, and handed potato blossoms to the royals - Louis XVI wore one in his lapel, Marie Antoinette wore them in her hair. His name lives on in 'hachis Parmentier,' the French cottage pie made with mashed potato. Sources: atlasobscura.com/articles/history-of-potatoes-parmentier; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Antoine-Augustin_Parmentier.  (Legend.)

question: A Roman host welcomes his guests to a formal dinner. To modern eyes, the oddest thing is how everyone eats — what posture did a Roman hold all through the meal?
context: Romans reclined on couches set around a low table, treating a long, leisurely meal as a mark of the civilized life; slaves brought each course to the diners. Source: Smith's Dictionary of Greek & Roman Antiquities, 'Triclinium' (LacusCurtius); Wikipedia, 'Triclinium.'

question: The Romans named their formal dining room after the broad couches that lined it — set in a U around a central table, with the open side left for slaves to serve. What was this couch-lined dining room called?
context: Triclinium literally means 'three couches': three broad couches held nine diners, three to a couch, with the open fourth side kept clear for serving. Source: Wikipedia, 'Triclinium'; UNRV, 'Triclinium.'

question: A popular story claims that rich Romans, stuffed from a feast, would stagger off to a special room called a 'vomitorium' to throw up and then return to eat more. The truth is far less disgusting — a vomitorium was actually what?
answer: A passageway that funnels crowds out of an arena
choices: A passageway that funnels crowds out of an arena
A side kitchen for preparing extra courses
A fountain room where guests rinsed their hands
A cellar where wine was chilled before serving
context: The word comes from Latin vomere, 'to spew forth' — describing how a packed amphitheatre 'spewed' its crowd out through the exits, not diners purging. No ancient source uses it for post-meal vomiting; the Colosseum had 80 such passages, emptying tens of thousands of spectators in minutes. Source: The Conversation, 'Mythbusting Ancient Rome — the truth about the vomitorium'; Wikipedia, 'Vomitorium.'

question: Reclining Roman diners always propped themselves up on their left elbow, keeping that arm pinned beneath them for the whole meal. Why tie up the left arm like that?
answer: It freed the right hand to reach for food
choices: It freed the right hand to reach for food
It turned the face toward the host of honor
It was believed to settle the stomach
It kept the fine dinner robes from creasing
context: With most people right-handed, lying on the left elbow left the stronger right hand free to take food from the low central table. Source: Smith's Dictionary of Greek & Roman Antiquities, 'Triclinium'; Wikipedia, 'Triclinium.'

question: Romans splashed their favorite condiment, garum, onto nearly everything — vegetables, roast meat, even fruit. It was the ketchup of their world. What was garum actually made from?
answer: Fish and salt, cured in the sun
choices: Fish and salt, cured in the sun
Grapes boiled down to a syrup
Olives crushed and pressed with herbs
context: Garum's deep savory kick came from glutamates released as the fish broke down — what we now call umami. The pungent sauce was so prized it was blended into named varieties: with pepper, with wine, even cut with water. Source: Wikipedia, 'Garum'; National Geographic, 'What Is Garum?'

question: A formal Roman dinner ran in three acts: the gustatio, an opening course famous for its eggs; then the main tables; and finally the secunda mensa. What did Romans bring out for that closing course?
context: So reliably did a meal run from an egg course to a fruit finish that the poet Horace summed up a whole dinner as 'ab ovo usque ad mala' — 'from egg to apples.' Source: Wikipedia, 'Ab ovo'; Wikipedia, 'Food in ancient Rome.'

question: The reclining banquet came to Rome from Greece, but the Romans changed one rule about who lay on the dining couches — a change that Greeks would have found scandalous. What was the Roman custom?
answer: Respectable women reclined right beside the men
choices: Respectable women reclined right beside the men
Guests reclined in strict order of wealth
Children reclined once they turned seven
Slaves reclined for the meal's final toast
context: At a Greek symposium the couches were male-only — the only women present were entertainers and servants. Roman wives and daughters dining openly beside men became a hallmark of the Roman banquet. Source: The Metropolitan Museum of Art, 'The Roman Banquet'; Wikipedia, 'Triclinium.'

question: In Petronius's satirical novel the Satyricon, a vulgar rich host named Trimalchio loves dishes that startle his guests. A whole roast hog is carried in, and Trimalchio erupts in fake fury that the cook forgot to gut it — so the cook carves it open right there at the table. What tumbles out?
answer: Cooked sausages and blood puddings, like its own innards
choices: Cooked sausages and blood puddings, like its own innards
Live thrushes, which burst free and flap off
Pastry eggs, hidden in a nest of straw
Hot spiced wine, gushing like a fountain
context: The Satyricon's feast is comic fiction, mocking a host who spends wildly to show off. Trimalchio pretends the cook forgot to gut the pig, then the belly is slit and sausages and blood puddings tumble out — one of several 'trick dishes' built purely to fool and delight the diners. Source: Petronius, Satyricon (Trimalchio's Feast), Fordham Ancient History Sourcebook.

question: At a rich Roman's feast, one prized appetizer was a whole roasted dormouse — a fat little rodent served as a luxury treat. How was this dormouse dressed up to impress the guests?
answer: Glazed in honey and rolled in poppy seeds
choices: Glazed in honey and rolled in poppy seeds
Stuffed with figs and wrapped in vine leaves
Simmered in fish sauce and dusted with pepper
Split, salted, and dried hard as a biscuit
context: The honey-and-poppy-seed dormouse appears as an hors d'oeuvre in Petronius's Satyricon. Romans thought dormice such decadent luxuries that a censor once passed a law banning them from the table, alongside shellfish and imported birds. Source: Atlas Obscura, 'The Dormouse-Fattening Jars of Ancient Rome'; Petronius, Satyricon.

question: Romans didn't just catch dormice for the table — they fattened them first. A farmer kept the dormice in the dark inside a special pierced earthenware pot, ribbed inside with little ramps and a food hollow and stuffed with acorns and chestnuts, until the sleepy rodents grew plump. What was this dormouse-fattening pot called?
context: Glirarium comes from glis, the Latin for dormouse. The dark, cramped jar mimicked a burrow so the dormice fattened fast; the cookbook of Apicius even preserves a recipe for stuffing them with pork, pepper, and pine nuts before roasting. Source: Atlas Obscura, 'The Dormouse-Fattening Jars of Ancient Rome'; Sarah E. Bond, 'Pass the Dormice.'

question: People treat salt like a guilty pleasure, but your body would fail within minutes without it. The sodium in salt has one life-or-death job. What is that job?
answer: It carries the electrical signal behind every nerve and muscle.
choices: It carries the electrical signal behind every nerve and muscle.
It builds the hard mineral structure of bones and teeth.
It ferries oxygen from your lungs out to your tissues.
It clots the blood to seal and close a wound.
context: Sodium is an essential electrolyte. Every time a nerve fires, sodium ions rush into the cell to create the electrical signal, and that same signal tells muscle cells to contract, so without sodium you could not think a thought or twitch a finger. Salt is a genuine need, not just a vice. Source: med.libretexts.org, Nutrition Science and Everyday Application (Callahan, Leonard & Powell), 8.05.

question: Salt was once so precious that caravans of as many as 40,000 camels hauled it 400 miles across the Sahara Desert. In the markets on the desert's far side, merchants would swap salt for an equal weight of one other treasure. Pound for pound, what did they trade their salt for?
context: In the medieval Sahel south of the Sahara, salt was so scarce it could be worth its weight in gold, while the region overflowed with gold but had little salt, making the trade fabulously lucrative. Rome had earlier guarded its own 150-mile Via Salaria, the 'Salt Road,' just to move the stuff. This is romanticized history: the camel numbers and the exact weight-for-weight gold swap are traditional accounts. Source: time.com, 'A Brief History of Salt.'  (Legend.)

question: Table salt looks like one simple ingredient, but chemically it's a compound: two different elements bonded into every tiny crystal. A cook who knows this understands why nutrition labels track only one of the two. Which two elements make up table salt?
context: Table salt is sodium chloride, NaCl. By weight it's about 40% sodium and 60% chloride, and it's only the sodium half that the whole health debate is about, which is why a food label says 'sodium,' not 'salt.' One teaspoon of table salt carries roughly 2,300 mg of sodium. Source: cdc.gov, 'About Sodium and Health.'

question: For decades, U.S. dietary guidelines urged nearly every adult to cut back on salt, warning that too much sodium raises blood pressure, a real danger for salt-sensitive people. The warning rests on simple physics. Once extra sodium is in your blood, what does it physically do to push the pressure up?
answer: It pulls water into the bloodstream, swelling the blood's volume.
choices: It pulls water into the bloodstream, swelling the blood's volume.
It stiffens the artery walls so they can no longer flex.
It signals the heart to beat faster and harder than normal.
It thickens the blood into a slower, stickier fluid.
context: This is the reduction side's strongest case. Sodium draws water with it, so more sodium in the blood means more blood volume and higher pressure, hitting salt-sensitive and hypertensive people hardest. The American Heart Association pushes an even stricter 1,500 mg ideal; as the AHA's Dr. Frank Sacks put it, 'Most Americans are consuming more sodium than their body needs. Lowering sodium intake lowers blood pressure, which can save lives.' Source: nutritionsource.hsph.harvard.edu, 'Salt and Sodium'; tctmd.com.

question: Health advice long assumed one simple rule: the less salt, the better. Then the PURE study tracked about 94,000 people across 18 countries for years, weighing their sodium against their heart risk. Its authors reported what actually happened at the LOW end of salt intake. What did the data suggest about people who ate very little salt?
answer: Their risk crept back up, as if too little salt were harmful too.
choices: Their risk crept back up, as if too little salt were harmful too.
Their risk kept dropping in a steady line, the lowest of all.
Their risk stayed flat, unchanged no matter how low they went.
Their risk fell by roughly half compared with heavy salters.
context: The PURE data traced a J-SHAPED curve: heart risk climbed clearly only above roughly 5 grams of sodium a day, but below a healthy middle the curve bent back UP. Lead author Andrew Mente concluded 'about 3 to 5 grams per day appears to be the optimal level associated with lowest risk,' so the honest takeaway is 'there's a healthy middle,' not 'less is always better.' Big caveat: this comes from observational data and is contested. The AHA's Frank Sacks argues sick people may already eat less salt (reverse causation) and that a single urine sample is a shaky measure, and population-reduction bodies hold that lowering everyone's salt still saves lives. Read it as 'evidence suggests a middle range,' not settled fact. Source: The Lancet (Mente, O'Donnell, Yusuf et al., 2018); tctmd.com.  (Legend.)

question: A home cook decides to eat less sodium, so they put down the salt shaker. A dietitian says that barely moves the needle: for the average American, only a small slice of daily sodium is the salt they add themselves, and around 70% is already IN the food before it reaches the kitchen. Which foods hide most of that built-in sodium?
answer: Packaged and restaurant food — breads, cheeses, cold cuts, canned soup.
choices: Packaged and restaurant food — breads, cheeses, cold cuts, canned soup.
Naturally salty whole foods — celery, beets, and fresh shellfish.
Fresh fruit — bananas, oranges, ripe melons, and berries.
Raw meats and seafood — fresh chicken, beef, and white fish.
context: The CDC and FDA estimate that roughly 70% (surveys run 70-77%) of Americans' sodium is built into processed, packaged, and restaurant food: breads, cheeses, cold cuts, canned soups. The sneaky part is that many of them, like bread and cookies, don't even taste salty. So salting your own whole-food cooking from scratch is a small slice of the total, and it's the slice a cook can actually control. Source: fda.gov, 'Sodium Reduction in the Food Supply.'

question: It's easy to guess the sandwich got its name because two slices of bread 'sandwich' a filling in the middle. In truth, the food was named after ___?
context: The food is named for John Montagu, the 4th Earl of Sandwich (1718-1792), an English aristocrat and politician. Curiously, it took his aristocratic TITLE, not his family name (Montagu) -- otherwise we might be ordering a 'montagu' for lunch. Source: HISTORY, 'Who Invented the Sandwich?'; Wikipedia, 'John Montagu, 4th Earl of Sandwich.'

question: The 4th Earl of Sandwich didn't dream up his title's odd name himself. Long before it ever labelled a lunch, 'Sandwich' was ___?
answer: an old seaport town in Kent
choices: an old seaport town in Kent
a card game played at court
an old English word for bread
context: The earldom was created in 1660 for the naval commander Edward Montagu, the 1st Earl, who chose 'Sandwich' as a compliment to the town in Kent his fleet lay off when it sailed to bring Charles II back to England. So the food is named after a man, who was named after a town. Source: Wikipedia, 'Earl of Sandwich.'

question: As the legend goes, around 1762 the Earl of Sandwich was so absorbed in a marathon card game that he wouldn't leave the table to eat. He had cooked meat brought between two slices of bread for one simple reason -- so that ___?
answer: he could eat one-handed and keep the cards free of grease
choices: he could eat one-handed and keep the cards free of grease
he could tuck it away and nibble between hands
he could hand the same meal to his fellow players
he could eat without the servants noticing
context: The gambling-table tale traces to a gossipy French travel writer, Pierre-Jean Grosley, in 'A Tour to London' (early 1770s). Other gamblers supposedly began ordering 'the same as Sandwich,' and the name stuck. Tellingly, Grosley never actually named the Earl of Sandwich -- readers just assumed it was him. Source: HISTORY, 'Who Invented the Sandwich?'; historyhit.com, 'Did the 4th Earl of Sandwich Really Invent the Sandwich?'  (Legend.)

question: The colorful tale of the Earl gambling for a whole day may be too good to be true. His own biographer notes that John Montagu spent three terms as First Lord of the Admiralty, running Britain's navy, and was buried in duties day and night. So historians now suspect the first 'sandwich' was really eaten ___?
choices: on the deck of a warship at sea
at a grand banquet in London
at a roadside inn while travelling
context: The earliest written use of 'sandwich' is in historian Edward Gibbon's 1762 diary, describing gentlemen at the Cocoa Tree coffeehouse supping 'upon a bit of cold meat, or a Sandwich' -- and it says nothing about gambling. Biographer N.A.M. Rodger argues a quick one-handed meal at the busy official's desk fits far better than a 24-hour card binge. Source: historyhit.com, 'Did the 4th Earl of Sandwich Really Invent the Sandwich?'; wordorigins.org; Wikipedia, 'John Montagu, 4th Earl of Sandwich.'

question: The Earl gave the food its English NAME, but people had eaten meat between bread for ages before him. About 1,800 years earlier, a Jewish sage was already wrapping Passover lamb and bitter herbs inside flatbread -- a mouthful still eaten at the Seder today. Who was he?
context: Around the 1st century BC, Hillel the Elder combined the Passover lamb, matzah, and bitter herbs in one bite. Jews still eat it at the Seder as the 'Korech,' or 'Hillel sandwich' -- and 'Korech' comes from a root meaning to wrap or embrace, a literal description of a sandwich centuries before the English word existed. So the Earl gave the world the name, not the invention. Source: HISTORY, 'Who Invented the Sandwich?'; Chabad.org; thejc.com, 'Karich.'

question: A cook notices the butter, lard, and cheese sitting as firm blocks on the counter, while the olive oil and corn oil pour like water. That habit of staying solid at room temperature is a rough giveaway that a fat is mostly which type?
context: Butter, lard, beef tallow, and cheese are all high in saturated fat and stay solid or semi-solid at room temperature, while the liquid cooking oils — olive, corn, soybean — are mostly unsaturated and stay liquid. The 'solid vs liquid at room temp' test is a rough sort for saturated vs unsaturated fat. Source: Wikipedia, 'Saturated fat.'

question: Most cooking oils pour freely and are mostly unsaturated fat. But one common oil breaks the pattern: in a cool kitchen it turns solid and waxy, because about 87% of its fat is saturated — higher even than butter or lard. Which oil is the odd one out?
context: Coconut oil is the odd one out: it's a PLANT fat, yet about 87% of its fat is saturated — higher than butter or lard — which is why it turns solid or semi-solid at room temperature like animal fat instead of pouring like other vegetable oils. Source: Wikipedia, 'Saturated fat.'

question: A food lab measured the saturated fat in four everyday cooking fats. Which one turned out to be the MOST saturated of the group?
context: About two-thirds of butter's fat (~63%) is saturated, and cheese is similar (~64%). By contrast, pork lard is about 39% saturated and beef tallow about 41% — so those greasy animal fats are actually LESS saturated than the butter on your toast. Source: Wikipedia, 'Saturated fat' fat-composition table.

question: Even the scientists who call the old fear of butter overblown agree the old view got ONE thing right: eating a lot of saturated fat reliably pushes up one of the measurements your doctor takes at a checkup. Which one climbs?
context: The mechanism behind the old advice is real and still holds: saturated fat raises LDL cholesterol (the 'bad' kind). The AHA states its rationale rests on the 'well-established effects of saturated fat to raise low-density lipoprotein (LDL) cholesterol, a leading cause of atherosclerosis.' Source: Wikipedia, 'Saturated fat and cardiovascular disease,' quoting the AHA.

question: In 1958, American physiologist Ancel Keys set out to prove that saturated fat was clogging people's arteries. He launched a huge, long-running project that tracked the diets and heart health of thousands of middle-aged men, and it became the scientific backbone of the entire anti-fat era. What is that landmark study remembered as today?
context: The idea traces to Ancel Keys and his 'diet-heart hypothesis' from the early 1950s: he argued saturated fat raised blood cholesterol, which caused heart disease. In 1958 he launched the Seven Countries Study, tracking middle-aged men across the USA, Finland, the Netherlands, Italy, Yugoslavia, Greece, and Japan. Source: Seven Countries Study (sevencountriesstudy.com); Wikipedia, 'Ancel Keys.'

question: 'Bad' LDL cholesterol isn't one single thing — it rides through the blood as particles of different sizes and densities. Researchers who sorted those particles found that eating a lot of saturated fat nudges a person's LDL toward one particular kind. Which kind does saturated fat tend to produce?
context: Later research added nuance the old story missed: saturated fat also raises HDL (the 'good' cholesterol), and it tends to shift LDL toward larger, buoyant particles rather than the small, dense ones more strongly tied to heart risk. It's the same LDL number telling a more complicated story. Source: Krauss/LDL particle-size research; PLOS One 2017, 'Effects of a very high saturated fat diet on LDL particles.'

question: Here's the bitter irony of the anti-butter decades: the margarine and shortening people switched to in order to protect their hearts were made by forcing hydrogen through liquid vegetable oil until it stiffened into a spreadable block. That process reworked the oil's fat molecules. What kind of fat was hiding in the old margarine?
context: People told to ditch butter for margarine were often getting something worse. Early margarine and shortening were made with partially hydrogenated oils loaded with TRANS fat — the one fat later research pinned clearly to heart disease. Chowdhury's 2014 meta-analysis found trans fat carried about 16% higher coronary risk while saturated fat showed essentially no clear link — the fat everyone feared and the fat that replaced it had swapped roles. Source: diet-history sources on hydrogenated-oil margarine; Chowdhury R et al. 2014, Annals of Internal Medicine.

question: In 2010, scientists pooled 21 separate studies covering nearly 348,000 people — the biggest test yet of whether saturated fat drives heart disease. Decades of dietary advice hung on what the numbers said. What did the analysis report?
answer: no clear link between saturated fat and heart disease
choices: no clear link between saturated fat and heart disease
a strong link between saturated fat and heart disease
a clear link between saturated fat and stroke alone
a link only among people who also ate lots of sugar
context: The 2010 turning point: Siri-Tarino's pooled analysis in the American Journal of Clinical Nutrition combined 21 studies and 347,747 people (11,006 of whom developed heart disease or stroke) and found saturated fat intake was NOT associated with increased risk of coronary heart disease, stroke, or cardiovascular disease. Source: Siri-Tarino PW et al. 2010, Am J Clin Nutr 91:535-546 (PubMed 20071648). The honest bottom line, though: those big analyses weakened the direct saturated-fat-to-heart-disease link, so guidelines eased — but Harvard's nutrition experts called the 'fat type doesn't matter' takeaway misleading. The fair verdict is 'the simple artery-clogging story was OVERSTATED,' NOT 'saturated fat is proven harmless' — the LDL rise is still real; it's the hard disease OUTCOME that's contested. Today WHO, AHA, and NHS still suggest keeping saturated fat under about 10% of daily calories. Source: Harvard T.H. Chan Nutrition Source critique; Wikipedia, 'Saturated fat and cardiovascular disease.'

question: The reversal didn't go unchallenged. In 2017 the American Heart Association fired back with a major report, pointing to careful trials where people who replaced butter and lard with a certain oil cut their heart-disease risk by about a third — a drop the AHA compared to taking a cholesterol-lowering statin. Which oil earned that praise?
context: The 2017 AHA Presidential Advisory (Sacks et al., in Circulation) held the line: randomized trials swapping saturated fat for polyunsaturated vegetable oil cut cardiovascular disease by about 30% — a reduction the authors compared to statin drugs. This is the strongest steel-man FOR the old view. Source: Sacks FM et al. 2017, 'Dietary Fats and Cardiovascular Disease,' AHA Presidential Advisory, Circulation.

question: From a mild jalapeño slice to the fieriest pepper on Earth, a chili's entire burn comes from one single chemical the plant makes. Name that chemical.
context: It's capsaicin. Whether a chili is barely warm or a record-smashing monster, this one compound is the source of all the heat — and its concentration is exactly what the Scoville scale, invented by pharmacist Wilbur Scoville in 1912, was built to measure. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scoville_scale; nist.gov, 'How do you measure the heat of a pepper?'

question: Bite into something way too spicy and your instinct is to gulp water — but water actually makes the burn feel WORSE, smearing the oily capsaicin around instead of rinsing it away. What cold drink truly calms the fire?
context: Cold milk. Because capsaicin is an oil, water just spreads it across your mouth; a protein in milk called casein grabs the oily capsaicin and carries it off your nerve endings. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Capsaicin.

question: In 2005, scientists confirmed the very first chili pepper ever to blast past one MILLION Scoville heat units — roughly 170 times hotter than a bottle of Tabasco sauce. What is this record-breaking chili called?
context: The ghost pepper, or bhut jolokia. Paul Bosland's Chile Pepper Institute at New Mexico State University measured it at about 1,001,304 SHU using HPLC, and Guinness crowned it the world's hottest pepper in 2007. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bhut_jolokia.

question: Capsaicin never raises your mouth's temperature by even one degree — hold a thermometer to your tongue and nothing is hot. Yet the sensation is unbearable. Its trick is to switch on one specific nerve sensor. What job is that sensor actually meant to do?
answer: warn you that you're touching something dangerously hot
choices: warn you that you're touching something dangerously hot
tell you when a food has turned bitter or spoiled
sense when your mouth has gone freezing cold
feel the sharp sting of a cut or a scrape
context: It hijacks your real heat alarm. Capsaicin latches onto a receptor called TRPV1 — the very one that fires when you touch something hotter than about 43°C — so your brain screams 'burning!' even though nothing is actually hot. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Capsaicin; ncbi.nlm.nih.gov, PMC6966804.

question: Everybody 'knows' the fieriest part of a chili is its seeds, so cooks scrape them out to tame a dish. But the seeds themselves make no capsaicin at all. Where is a pepper's heat really concentrated?
answer: in the pale ribs lining the inner wall
choices: in the pale ribs lining the inner wall
in the green stem and cap
context: In the pale, spongy ribs — the placental tissue — that run along the inner wall where the seeds attach; the seeds only taste hot because they've been pressed against that tissue. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Capsaicin.

question: Some people love fiercely spicy food so much they keep chasing hotter peppers — sweating, teary-eyed, but grinning through the 'chili high.' The pain of the burn actually makes your brain release a surge of its own feel-good chemicals, the same ones behind a runner's high. What are they called?
context: Endorphins, the body's own natural painkillers. Your brain floods them out to fight the pain of the capsaicin burn, and that pleasurable rush is a big reason heat-lovers keep coming back for more. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Capsaicin.

question: A wild chili plant pours energy into making capsaicin, a chemical that turns its own ripe fruit painful to eat — which sounds self-defeating. But biologists say the heat is really a shield guarding one part of the plant. What is the burn protecting?
answer: its seeds, from animals that would chew them up
choices: its seeds, from animals that would chew them up
its leaves, from swarms of hungry caterpillars
its roots, from burrowing underground pests
its flowers, from an early frost
context: Its seeds. Capsaicin evolved as a chemical weapon to drive off seed-crushing mammals — whose grinding molars would destroy the seeds — and to fight seed-rotting fungi. The heat is a defense, not an accident. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Capsaicin.

question: A chili's fiery capsaicin drives off most animals that try to eat it — yet one group of creatures gulps down whole peppers and feels no burn at all, because their nerves simply don't respond to capsaicin. They swallow the fruit and scatter the seeds, unharmed, in their droppings. Which animals are the pepper's chosen seed-carriers?
context: Birds. The receptor that capsaicin fools in mammals doesn't react to it in birds at all, so they feel nothing. A mammal would grind the seeds to bits with its molars — but a bird swallows them whole and plants them, intact, wherever it flies. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Capsaicin.

question: For a solid decade the Carolina Reaper reigned as the Guinness-certified hottest pepper alive. Then in 2023 the very breeder who created the Reaper, American Ed Currie, dethroned his own champion with an even fiercer chili he'd spent years crossbreeding. What did Currie name the new record-holder?
context: Pepper X. Grown by Currie's PuckerButt Pepper Company in South Carolina, it averaged about 2,693,000 SHU when Winthrop University tested it — far above the Reaper's ~1.64 million — and it's a cross of a Carolina Reaper with a pepper a friend had sent him.
